sections.h2: How does Louisiana property tax work?
sections.html:
Louisiana property tax is built locally: a parish assessor sets the value, local voters approve the millage rates, and the parish sheriff usually collects the bill. The state constitution fixes the assessment percentages, and the Louisiana Tax Commission hears the appeals that come up from local boards.

Louisiana has parishes where most states have counties. Wikipedia's Louisiana article notes it is one of only two states without counties, and it reports a 2020 census population of 4,657,757. For a seller that means the office you deal with is the parish assessor and the parish sheriff, whether the house is in New Orleans, Baton Rouge or a small town.

The East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff's office puts the division of labor plainly: the sheriff does not decide how much you owe. The assessed value comes from the assessor, and the millage comes from votes by residents of the parish.

sections.h2: What percentage of value is taxed in Louisiana?
sections.html:
Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value, while other property is assessed at 15%. Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution sets these levels, and it also sets 25% for public service property other than land.

Property typeAssessment level
Land10%
Residential improvements10%
Other property15%
Public service property (not land)25%

Property must be reappraised at intervals of no more than four years. When a reappraisal pushes the assessed value of a homestead-exempt house up by more than 50% over the year before, the added tax is phased in over four years. That phase-in ends when the property changes hands, so a buyer may face the full figure that a long-time owner never paid. The constitution also holds the assessment level for qualifying owners, including those 65 or older, subject to an income limit.

The legislature's text of section 18 has the full wording.

sections.h2: How is a Louisiana tax bill calculated, with an example?
sections.html:
Take the fair market value, subtract any homestead exemption, apply the 10% level, then multiply by the total millage. The St. James Parish Assessor posts worked examples that show every step.

StepExample 1Example 2
Fair market value$100,000$150,000
Less homestead exemption$75,000$75,000
Taxable value$25,000$75,000
Assessed value at 10%$2,500$7,500
Bill at 10.703 percent millage$267.58$802.73

That parish's page uses a 10.703 percent rate for illustration, and rates differ from parish to parish and from one tax district to the next. The same page points out how sharply the bill moves: because the $75,000 exemption stays fixed, each extra $25,000 of value adds $267.58 in its example. Look at the assessor's page to see the layout.

The East Baton Rouge sheriff adds a caution. The homestead exemption covers parish taxes only, so city taxes and fire or crime fees are still owed on the full amount.

sections.h2: What does the homestead exemption cover?
sections.html:
The homestead exemption removes parish property tax on the first $75,000 of a home's market value, which is $7,500 of assessed value. Owners must apply with the parish assessor, and the home must be their primary residence.

  • It applies to one home per owner.
  • The East Baton Rouge Parish Assessor says the owner must own and occupy the residence by December 31 of the tax year.
  • It does not reduce city taxes or fire and crime district fees in East Baton Rouge Parish.
  • A tax sale can cost the owner the exemption.

For sellers this matters in an odd way. The exemption attaches to an owner who lives in the home, so a buyer who will not occupy it would not qualify. That means your current bill may understate what the next owner pays. A seller who is asked about taxes should say so plainly.

sections.h2: When are Louisiana property taxes due, and what happens after?
sections.html:
Taxes for the year are due by December 31, and the roll normally reaches the collector by November 15. The sheriff mails bills in the last week of November, and the St. James assessor's page gives the same schedule.

  • After December 31 the taxes are delinquent, and interest runs at 1% per month.
  • The East Baton Rouge sheriff adds a collection fee if taxes are unpaid after January 31, followed by certified notice and advertising costs.
  • La. R.S. 47:2153 has the tax collector send certified mail by the first Monday of February, with 20 days to pay before the lien is auctioned.
  • A deposit of up to $1,000 may be required from bidders.

Louisiana's newer process auctions a tax lien before it auctions the house. The winning bidder gets a recorded tax lien certificate. The owner keeps ownership and possession until a court judgment is executed, and during that time the lienholder may not evict the owner or collect rent. To get the lien released, the owner pays the auction price, interest of up to 1% a month, a 5% penalty and costs, and this can be done any time before an enforcement action is filed.

The EBR sheriff's FAQ describes the older tax sale process, under which a property sold could be redeemed within three years from recordation with a 5% penalty plus 1% interest a month. Parishes may differ on timing, so check which process your parish runs.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Louisiana property assessment?
sections.html:
You start with the parish assessor and the board of review, and only then go to the Louisiana Tax Commission and district court. Each step has a short window, so owners who wait lose the chance.

StepWhat the statute says
Request a written notice of assessmentAsk no earlier than June 1; the assessor must receive it by June 15 (R.S. 47:1992)
Inspection of the roll15 days between August 15 and September 15 in most parishes; July 15 to August 15 in Orleans
Board of review complaintGive the board at least seven days' notice; the board may raise or lower the value
Appeal to the Tax CommissionHearings begin within ten days of receiving the certified lists (R.S. 47:1989)
District courtFile within thirty days of the commission's decision

The board of review must convene hearings on or before September 15 and certify its list to the Tax Commission by October 20, and the assessor certifies the rolls to the board on or before October 1. The Tax Commission may affirm, remand, reverse or modify an assessment. A taxpayer who sues pays the disputed amount under protest, and under R.S. 47:1998 the undisputed part is paid without protest.

The statutes are on Justia: R.S. 47:1992 and R.S. 47:1989.

sections.h2: What happens to property taxes when you sell a house in Louisiana?
sections.html:
Taxes follow the property, and the sheriff does not split them between buyer and seller. The East Baton Rouge sheriff states that tax, interest, penalties and fees stay in effect until paid regardless of who owns the property, and that any private agreement between the two sides does not bind the collector.

A sale after January 1 can leave the bill in the previous owner's name on the roll, because the assessor sets values as of January 1. The buyer must still check whether taxes are owed. Louisiana also lets an assessor add omitted property for up to three back years under R.S. 47:1966, so a house missing from the roll can generate a catch-up bill.

  • Ask the sheriff's tax office for the account balance before listing or signing.
  • Settle the current year's bill at closing and put the split in writing.
  • Under R.S. 9:2721, the deed names the person responsible for property taxes and the address for notices, so that detail must be right.
  • Confirm the homestead exemption status with the assessor.

If back taxes are already piling up, we can look at the house as it stands and explain how the payoff would work at closing.

faqs.q: What is the Louisiana homestead exemption?
faqs.a: It removes parish property tax on the first $75,000 of a primary residence's value, which is $7,500 of assessed value. You apply through the parish assessor. City taxes and fire or crime fees in East Baton Rouge are not covered.

faqs.q: When are Louisiana property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due by December 31 of the tax year. Bills are mailed in late November, and interest at 1% a month starts after December 31. A collection fee and advertising costs can follow after January 31.

faqs.q: What percent of value is a Louisiana home assessed at?
faqs.a: Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value under Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution. Other property is assessed at 15%. Reappraisal must happen at least every four years.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Louisiana house with back taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes, but the taxes are paid out of the proceeds or by the buyer at closing, since they stay attached to the property. A recorded tax lien must be cleared before clean title passes. The sheriff will give you a payoff figure.

faqs.q: How do I dispute my Louisiana assessment?
faqs.a: Ask the assessor for the notice, then bring a complaint to the parish board of review during its hearing window. A board decision can be appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and then to district court within thirty days of the commission's decision.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Louisiana?
faqs.a: The parish sheriff, acting as tax collector, sends and collects the bills. The parish assessor sets the value, and local voters approve the millage rates.
